utterance_src: اگه پول نباشه مشلکی نیست. اصلا قابل شما ره نداره!
context: Speaker: Seller to any buyer who might have bought groceries from the shop.
literal_render: If you have no money, it is totally fine. My grocery is not worth you.
intent_render: Unless you are really going some unprecendent financial burden, which if true we could talk about more, I expect to get the agree upon price. -- This is a first no among grocery shops in Kabul.
pragmatic_note: If read literally, it come across as the seller just handing back the money! However, that is just ritualistic politeness and the seller still does expect to get the full price of the good.

utterance_src:
- یک پیاله چای بنوشید. 
- نه تشکر تازه صبحانه خوردم.
context: The host of a shop is speaking to a client who has come to their shop and is offering them tea.
literal_render:
- Please have a cup of tea.
- No thanks I just had breakfast.
intent_render:
- Please have a cup of tea
- I really appreciate your offer. Could you insist one more time for me to get a pass at the ritualistic process of interaction and then finally accept your offer.
pragmatic_note: The no thanks I had breakfast part, which even if it might empirically be true, is still a first 'no'. The speaker should insist.

utterance_src: ده ای روزها یک مقدار دستم تنگ شده. اگه پیشت کدام مبلغ از همو بیست هزاری که دو ماه پیش داده بودم باشه خیلی عالی میشه.
context: Cousin is speaker to another cousin and asking for if they could get a repayment for the 20k Afghani loan that they paid to them earlier.
literal_render: In these days, my hands have become a bit tight. It would be great if you had some amount from the 20000 Afghanis I had lent you earlier.
intent_render: I need the money that I had lent you two months ago. Could you please repay me the 20k amount?
pragmatic_note: Here the ask has been turned from a question into a sentence that states the hope of the lender. However, the ask is best considered an explicit request for the total repayment of the money.

utterance_src: ان‌شاءالله ببینیم که خدا چه میخواهه.
context: A group of elders is asking their district mayor if they could enforce a policy and ask for resources from the government to solve the lack of drinking water issues in their neighborhood.
literal_render: God willing, we will see what God wants.
intent_render: I don't think I can or am willing to focus on this task at hand.
pragmatic_note: Inshallah is used in many ways, in the US and among Western muslims it is considered as an expression of hope for something to happen. However, given the tone, it also usually means that the person speaking won't personally take responsibility to do anything and leave it to some other force to take a stab at it.

utterance_src: من بازار ره میگردم باز دوباره خدمت تان میایم.
context: Customer is talking to a fabric seller after asking for the price and quality of the fabric.
literal_render: I will wander around the bazaar and come back to you.
intent_render: I think I won't buy the fabric.
pragmatic_note: Taken at its face value it seems like the customer is making a promise - namely that they will be back. However, this is an easy way for the customer to not buy the good, without making the social interaction awkward from within the social framework that has already been set up.

context: A tailor is presenting a custom-made dress to their client.
literal_render: It is not at all worthy of you.
intent_render: Mild self-deprecation intending to tell the client that they are worthy of great things.
pragmatic_note: If read literally, the text sounds too deprecative. However, it is meant to actually be a compliment to the buyer of the dress.

utterance_src: شرمنده تان استم خلیفه. رویم سیاه. پول تان ره تا هفته دیگه جور میکنم.
context: A customer who has borrowed money almost a year ago now is talking to their lender in their shop.
literal_render: I am ashamed of being in your presence Khalifa, (Caliph). My face is black. I will surely prepare your money until next week.
intent_render: I am sorry and I have some feelings of guilt for not having paid your money until now. I will do my best to do it soon. Khalifa here is a common phrase you would call anyone, like people calling each other "cuh" in the US or "mate".
pragmatic_note: The first two sentences don't translate well in English because they're more of phrases than formal language.

utterance_src: کاکا جان حرف تان روی دیده. هرچند من یک گفتنی کوچک داشتم.
context: Niece is talking to his uncle and is thinking of phrasing a disagreement about the uncle's proposal that involves some requests from the niece's parents and siblings.
literal_render: Dear uncle, your words' place are on my two eyes. However, I had a small thing I would like to add.
intent_render: Dear uncle, although I have complete request for you and would like to accept your proposal, I do have some objections that I would like to raise first.
pragmatic_note: If read literally it could come across as adding more context or note, and not as a sort of disagreement that the niece is trying to present.
